title: Release of "Walking the Blues" and Bob Rolontz's Groove label
summary: King added a rhythm section to the tape and released it; RCA's new Groove label then invited McRae to record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: So he got that rhythm section out there. They stayed in the studio all day. Had a house band. They were just backing up different singers soming through, you know.
So they put the rhythm to it. They put on earphones and put the rhythm to it and release it called 'Walking The Blues.'

And then, why we got down to RCA Victor, Bob Rolontz had (inaudible) with different companies -- RCA Victor had called him in and named this Groove Records. He had put out (inaudible) RCA called Groove Records.
He didn't know anything about -- He heard -- he knew me and I saw him on the street, and he say, "What're you doing? Hear you got a hit record."
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I say, "Yeah." He says, "Are you signed with King?" I says, "No." He says, "Jack signed with King?" I say, "No, Jack ain't signed -- he just record over there." He says, "You wanna make a date with us?" I say, "Yeah."
So we went down and we made this "Lonely Road Blues" with him. Jack made a couple of sides. Jack made a couple of more things with him by himself.
In the meanwhile, he called me up again. He wanted me to do a date on my own -- "Mr. Bear" -- do my own dates since the record was big, you know.
Walking The Blues was big. Jack Dupree and "Mr. Bear" was a big selling record.
